description: I'm a student who is interesting in building games.
summary:
Space Frontier is a browser-based, third-person astronaut adventure and educational simulation. Choose the Moon or Mars, then watch your spacecraft lose engine power and make an emergency landing. On the surface, follow mission objectives across a 3D outpost, cycle through airlocks, and repair the equipment that keeps the habitat running.

Survival depends on managing suit oxygen, electrical power, water, food, and spare parts. Repairs are hands-on. You reconnect cables, turn valves, replace filters, and clean solar contacts. Beyond the habitat, you can drive a rover, drill for ice, salvage components, collect research samples, and tow stranded robots back to base. Recovered supplies and research help you build upgrades such as a solar canopy, water recovery tanks, and a field workshop. During emergencies, you can radio Earth for advice and prepare the shelter. To complete the expedition, fabricate a return rocket, reach the launch pad, and head home.

Junior Explorer mode introduces the controls and repairs through a playable tutorial that pauses resource consumption. Specialist mode gives players more direct control over outpost systems. The game uses real spaceflight concepts such as pressure cycling, oxygen production, and communication delays. Missions save locally in your browser, so you can return to your expedition later.
details:
Space Frontier is a browser-based astronaut adventure that teaches players how to keep a Moon or Mars outpost running. After an emergency landing, players explore a 3D landscape, repair habitat equipment, and manage oxygen, water, food, power, and spare parts. They drive rovers, drill for ice, collect research samples, and recover stranded robots. Their final goal is to build a rocket and return to Earth.

The project makes space science tangible through decisions players can see and act on. Running the greenhouse uses power that the habitat also needs for life support. Airlocks demonstrate why pressure must equalize before a door opens. Repair tasks turn system failures into hands-on puzzles: players reconnect cables, turn valves, replace filters, and clear dust from solar contacts. The intended impact is to help younger learners understand how astronauts solve problems with limited resources and how one decision can affect an entire outpost.

We built Space Frontier with TypeScript, React, Three.js, and Vite, used Vitest for automated testing, and deployed it through GitHub and Vercel. It runs in a browser with keyboard and mouse or on-screen touch controls, without a download or account.

Our team considered scientific accuracy, ease of learning, and performance on different devices. We simplified or shortened some processes for play and used in-game explanations to connect them to real spaceflight. The Junior Explorer tutorial pauses resource consumption so new players can practice safely, while Specialist mode gives players more control over outpost systems. Local saves let players explore at their own pace across multiple sessions.
